metadata.title: What Is a Gap-Surfacer Actually Looking For?
metadata.purpose: Answer what a checklist-vs-document gap check is actually looking for, and what a 'no match' from one actually means. Lands the carry-out that a no-match is a lead, not a verdict.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible gap-check account from the skill's name rather than lifting facts that were never written.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the assignment-clause checklist item: flagged with no match, then found under different wording -- 'Transfer of Rights')

beats.narration_text: Someone on a legal team asks if a contract review tool catches bad clauses. Wrong verb. What it actually does is scan for missing ones — it's a completeness check, not a quality check. Liam, in for Bear — here's how the machine works.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Does this contract have any bad clauses?', hesitates on 'bad', corrects to 'missing', lands the real question

props.text:
Does this contract
have any
bad clauses?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('bad' -> 'missing') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: The intuitive guess: it reads each clause and grades whether it's well drafted — a quality check. That's not the mechanism. Under the hood, its checklist carries line items — governing law, indemnification, and so on — and for each one, the tool asks a single yes/no question: does matching text appear anywhere in this document. Nothing else. They optimized for coverage at the expense of judgment.

shot.new_visual_element: A 'quality check' magnifying-glass card fades in, then is struck through; a checklist chip and a scan sweep across a document card replace it, ending on a lit MATCH

production_viz.label: Not a quality check
production_viz.mechanic: A card labelled 'QUALITY CHECK' with a magnifying-glass icon fades in above a document card of squiggled clause lines. It is struck through and fades out. A single checklist chip reading 'GOVERNING LAW' appears; a scan-line sweeps down the document and the chip lights up green with 'MATCH'. Caption: 'does matching text show up anywhere? that's the only question.'

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening, step by step: the checker walks the list one line at a time — governing law, indemnification, assignment — and for each, sweeps the whole document for matching text. Watch the anchor. The assignment line comes back with no match anywhere in the file. Flagged, not resolved. The scan reports absence-of-string, and that's as far as it can tell you on its own.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three checklist chips scanned in turn; the first two light green with MATCH, the third (ASSIGNMENT) ends dim and red-outlined with NO MATCH

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- walking the checklist
production_viz.mechanic: Three checklist chips fade in in a row: GOVERNING LAW, INDEMNIFICATION, ASSIGNMENT. A scan-line sweeps under each in turn. The first two light green with a small 'MATCH' label. THE ANCHOR: the third (ASSIGNMENT) stays dim, outlined in terracotta, labelled 'NO MATCH' -- it does not resolve and remains on screen. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Turns out the protection was there the whole time — filed under Transfer of Rights instead of Assignment, so the checklist's word-for-word search missed the synonym. That cuts both ways. A match only tells you the label showed up; it doesn't prove the clause is any good. A no-match only tells you the label didn't; it doesn't prove the coverage is gone. Either way, a person still opens the page and reads.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the dim NO MATCH card connects by arrow to a highlighted 'TRANSFER OF RIGHTS' clause elsewhere in the document and lights up; then splits into two both-directions cards

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- same coverage, different name
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIM 'ASSIGNMENT / NO MATCH' CARD RETURNS, identical placement. An arrow draws from it to a highlighted clause elsewhere reading 'TRANSFER OF RIGHTS'; the dim card lights up and relabels to 'ASSIGNMENT = TRANSFER OF RIGHTS (found)'. It splits into two cards: left reads 'MATCH' with 'GOOD ENOUGH' struck through beneath it, labelled 'match is not good enough'; right reads 'NO MATCH' with 'GONE' struck through beneath it, labelled 'no-match is not gone'.

beats.narration_text: A gap-surfacer doesn't hand you a verdict — it hands you a lead. A no-match is a lead, not a verdict. The read is still yours.

props.quote: A gap-surfacer doesn't hand you a verdict — it hands you a lead. A no-match is a lead, not a verdict. The read is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take a document you're responsible for and a short checklist of what it should contain. Ask Claude to scan for matches, flag every item with no match, and for each flag also check whether equivalent coverage might be sitting under different wording before calling it missing. Go deeper: run the same document twice — once strict-wording, once paraphrase-tolerant — and see which flags survive both. Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I have a document and a short checklist of things it's supposed to include. Scan the document, flag every checklist item with no matching text anywhere in it, and for each flag, tell me whether equivalent coverage might exist under different wording before calling it missing.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: Run the same document twice — once strict-wording (flag if the checklist term doesn't appear verbatim), once paraphrase-tolerant (flag only if no semantic equivalent appears). Compare the two flag sets. Which items survive both runs, and what does the difference tell you about which parts of the checklist depend on exact legal terms and which don't?
